newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan first to recognise Taleban Afghan govt.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan first to recognise Taleban Afghan govt.

text.p: Pakistan became the first country to recognise the Taleban Islamic movement's government in neighbouring Afghanistan on Sunday and urged other countries and organisations to do the same.

No country had previously recognised the Taleban government, set up in September last year when the purist Islamic militia captured the capital Kabul and went on to take control of almost all of the war-shattered country.

"I am happy to announce that the government of Pakistan has now decided to accord formal recognition to the new government of the Islamic State of Afghanistan," Pakistan Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told a news conference which followed Taleban's sweeping military gains in the north at the weekend.
He said Pakistan had previously withheld recognition to "give time for the promotion of a broad-based government through peaceful negotiations", Khan said.

"We feel that the new government fulfils all criteria for de jure recognition," he said. "It is now in effective control of most of the territory of Afghanistan and is representative of all ethnic groups in that country."

Afghanistan's seat at the United Nations has been kept by the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani since the Taleban takeover of Kabul on September 27, but its seat in the 54-nation Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) has been left vacant.

Khan said he hoped that after the latest developments, the United Nations, the OIC and other international organisations would "also take the just decision of recognising the new (Afghan) government", which he said now controlled 26 of Afghanistan's 32 provinces.
"We also hope that the international community will fulfil its responsibility for the reconstruction and economic development of the brotherly state of Afghanistan," he added.
Pakistan has often been accused by the ousted Afghan government of aiding the Taleban.

Islamabad has repeatedly denied the charge, saying it has no favourites among the warring Afghan factions, most of which were based in Pakistan during the Mujahideen guerrilla war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
Khan said Pakistan would continue to promote an intra-Afghan dialogue but told a questioner it would welcome the Taleban's capture of territory still held by opposition factions.
He said Pakistan would soon reopen its Kabul embassy, closed in September 1995 after being ransacked by demonstrators protesting against Islamabad's alleged support for the Taleban.

But he said the Pakistan ambassador to Afghanistan, accompanied by a media team, would first fly on Monday to the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif, the former opposition stronghold taken by Taleban and its allies on Saturday.
